title: Ajax and Total Football
text:
When Rinus Michels became coach of Ajax Amsterdam in 1965, the club was struggling near the bottom of the Dutch league. He brought strict discipline, much harder training and a new idea of how a team could play.

The approach became known as Total Football. Players were not tied to one position. If a defender pushed forward, a midfielder or forward dropped back to cover his place, so the shape of the team held even as individuals moved around it. Ajax pressed opponents high up the field, pushed its defensive line forward to squeeze space, and used the offside trap aggressively. It required every player to be comfortable on the ball and to read the game the same way as his teammates.

At the center was Johan Cruyff, a thin, brilliant forward from a working-class Amsterdam neighborhood near the stadium, who roamed wherever he was needed and directed the others on the field. Around him Michels built a squad largely raised in the club's own youth system.

Ajax reached the European Cup final in 1969 and lost. Then, under Michels and his successor Stefan Kovacs, they won it three years running, in 1971, 1972 and 1973. Michels took the same ideas to the Dutch national team, which reached the 1974 World Cup final playing the same fluid style and was widely seen as the best team of the tournament, even though it lost to West Germany.
lesson: When everyone understands the whole game, not just their own role, a team can adapt on the fly. Cross-training builds a team that cannot be easily broken.
people: Rinus Michels, Johan Cruyff, Stefan Kovacs
source: Club records; David Winner, Brilliant Orange (2000)
